title: Gin
lead: Juniper first: what makes gin gin, the styles on the back bar, and the classics built on it.

sections.name: What gin is
know: Juniper is the piney berry that has to lead every gin.
Botanicals like coriander and citrus peel build around it.
Not Vodka gin has to taste of juniper; vodka of almost nothing.
sections.source: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu); US TTB standards of identity, 27 CFR 5.143 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/5.143)

sections.name: Styles of gin

lines.label: In short
lines.text: From crisp and dry to soft and malty.

know: London Dry is crisp and juniper-forward. It can be made anywhere.
Old Tom is softer and a little sweeter.
Genever is made from malt wine, so it tastes malty.
Contemporary gins keep juniper but let other botanicals lead.
sections.source: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu)

keyPoints.line: is the piney berry that has to lead every gin.
like coriander and citrus peel build around it.
gin has to taste of juniper; vodka of almost nothing.

read.where: Gin is a spirit flavored with **juniper**, and juniper has to **lead** the taste. Other **botanicals** build around it: coriander, citrus peel, angelica root and more. That piney, herbal taste is what sets gin apart from vodka.
read.mixup: **Gin** and **vodka** both start as clean spirit. Gin has to taste of **juniper**; vodka shouldn’t taste of much at all.
read.sayIt: It’s gin-based: bright, piney and herbal.

keyPoints.line: is crisp and juniper-forward. It can be made anywhere.
is softer and a little sweeter.
is made from malt wine, so it tastes malty.
gins keep juniper but let other botanicals lead.

read.bigIdea: From crisp and dry to soft and malty.
read.where: **London Dry** is crisp and juniper-forward. **Plymouth** comes from Plymouth, England. **Old Tom** is softer and a little sweeter. **Genever**, from the Netherlands and Belgium, is made from **malt wine**, so it tastes malty. **Contemporary** gins keep juniper but let other botanicals lead, like cucumber or citrus.

stops.name: Contemporary
stops.text: Juniper is there, but **other botanicals** lead.

read.mixup: **London Dry** is a method, not a place: it can be made anywhere.
read.sayIt: This one’s a London Dry: crisp, with juniper up front.

keyPoints.line: gin and tonic: the most common gin call.
ask gin or vodka; gin is the classic.
vermouth goes in a martini, not sweet.
if they name the gin, ring in that one.

read.bigIdea: A G&T, or a martini their way.
read.where: The most common gin order is a **gin and tonic**. A **martini** is gin (or vodka) stirred with **dry vermouth** and served **up**, so when a guest just says “a martini,” ask **gin or vodka**. They may add **dry**, **dirty** or **with a twist**. If they name the gin, it’s a **call**.

stops.name: Gin and tonic
stops.text: Gin and **tonic** over ice, often with lime.

read.mixup: A martini takes **dry** vermouth. **Sweet** vermouth is for the Manhattan and the Negroni.
read.sayIt: Gin or vodka? And olives or a twist?

keyPoints.line: is gin, Campari and sweet vermouth, equal parts.
is gin, lemon, sugar and soda.
is gin, lemon and sugar, topped with Champagne.

read.where: Gin is the base of the **Martini**, the **Negroni** (gin, Campari and sweet vermouth), the **Gimlet** (gin, lime and sugar), the **Tom Collins** (gin, lemon, sugar and soda), the **French 75** (gin, lemon and sugar topped with Champagne) and the **Bee’s Knees** (gin, lemon and honey). A **dry** gin keeps a Martini crisp.
read.mixup: A **Negroni** is gin. Made with bourbon instead, it’s a **Boulevardier**.
read.sayIt: It’s gin-based: bright, botanical and dry.

sources: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu); US TTB standards of identity, 27 CFR 5.143 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/5.143); Common bar practice; Our book: the classic and house cocktail specs in this app. Facts taken from the Level 2 lessons, which cite them. Written for Mise, Nov 12, 2026.

unverified: Plymouth gin’s protected status has lapsed (per Wikipedia); we only say where it comes from.
Taste words (“soft”, “peppery”, “grassy”) are general bar descriptions, not from a rule. Bar lead to check them against our bottles.
How guests order (mixers, neat or on the rocks, shots) is common US bar usage, not a rule; bar lead to confirm the house wording.
